summary: Weekly POC sync focused on latency tuning for Acme Finance pilot. Reviewed latest TTFT numbers, streaming behavior, and sequence length tail effects. transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We've got 42 minutes on the calendar; main goal today is to go over the latency results and next tuning steps.
[00:12] Olivia (Customer - CTO): Thanks, Jordan. Quick note, we've had a few internal raises since last week — we want to see TTFT under 120ms for the chat flows at p95.
[00:22] Samantha (Redwood SE): Got it. We've been looking at two levers: streaming chunk size and kernel selection. Initial TTFT without streaming was around 200ms on the test model, down to ~140ms with streaming, but can still improve.
[00:35] Raj (Customer - Platform Eng): When you say streaming, do you mean server-side streaming or client-level chunking? We do client-side partial renders too.
[00:42] Samantha: Server-side streaming — we stream tokens as they're generated. The two impacts are TTFT (first token delay) and tail latency because of batching behavior.
[00:52] Maya (ML Eng): On our side, the variance spikes at longer sequence lengths; some user prompts hit 1.5k tokens and that seems to blow up p99 latency.
[01:05] Samantha: Right, sequence length distribution is a big factor. We saw that kernels optimized for shorter sequences (fused attention) outperform generic kernels at 512-1024, but at 1k+ the memory patterns cause swapping in the KV cache and GPU kernel choice changes.
[01:18] Jordan: Quick question — did the microbench use quantized weights or FP16?
[01:22] Samantha: These runs were FP16. We did a quick INT8 run but need to validate quality. INT8 helps us shrink kernel times but can add dequant overhead at first token.
[01:33] Raj: Any mis-trans above — sorry — any specific kernel names we should call out? Our infra folks will need to coordinate with whoever manages the GPU drivers.
[01:40] Samantha: Mostly cuBLAS/cuDNN for matmuls and a custom attention kernel; the runtime will pick between the optimized fused-attention kernel and a fallback generic kernel depending on seq len and batch. Sometimes it picks the fallback which increases latency.
[01:52] Olivia: Can Redwood force kernel selection? We can tolerate a bit more cost for consistent latency.
[01:58] Samantha: Yes, we can pin kernel profiles in Dedicated; we can set runtime hints — e.g., prefer fused-attention up to N tokens or force smaller batch windows to avoid fallback. There's a cost tradeoff.
[02:10] Raj: Speaking of cost, what does forcing fused kernels do to GPU utilization?
[02:14] Jordan: It can decrease throughput efficiency if you reduce batching, so unit cost per token can go up. That's why we recommend a few experiments — measure TTFT vs cost at target throughput.
[02:25] Maya: About KV cache — are we using prefix cache across requests for similar sessions? We're seeing re-computation on repeated prompts.
[02:32] Samantha: Current pilot uses ephemeral KV per request. We can enable prefix caching for session-based flows which reduces compute for repeated prefixes, but it adds memory pressure for large concurrent sessions.
[02:42] Raj: If we enable caching, what's the p95 improvement?
[02:46] Samantha: On our internal benchmarks with similar traffic patterns, prefix hits reduced token compute by ~35% and improved p95 TTFT by ~25% for session flows. But depends on hit rate.
[02:56] Jordan: Let's talk about the TTFT microbenchmark plan — SE will run a tight loop of cold-start and warm-stream tests with varying chunk sizes (16/32/64 tokens), and with kernel pinning flags.
[03:07] Samantha: I'll run cold start (brand new session), warm start (cached KV), and streaming enabled runs. We'll capture per-step latencies and exported profiler traces.
[03:16] Maya: Can you also capture the kernel selection logs? Our infra team wants to see when runtime fell back.
[03:21] Samantha: Yep, will enable verbose kernel selection log.
[03:25] Raj: Any notes about network — we run from our GCP region in us-east4; is network RTT a big part of TTFT?
[03:32] Jordan: Network is usually small for TTFT when the model is warm and streaming is enabled; the big chunk is compute for token 1, e.g., kernel launch time, tokenizer overhead. But we should measure from your edge to our nearest host to be sure.
[03:46] Olivia: About Dedicated vs Hosted — if we go Dedicated, can we get the kernel pinning and custom autoscale behavior?
[03:52] Jordan: Yes, Dedicated gives you control over kernel profiles, batch windows, and reserved GPU pools to reduce noisy neighbors. Hosted has some controls but less kernel pinning.
[04:00] Maya: Any security blockers on Dedicated? We're regulated — need SOC2, KMS integration, audit logs.
[04:06] Jordan: We'll include the security packet; Dedicated supports KMS integrations and syslog/audit exports. I'll include SOC2/ISO summaries in that packet.
[04:15] Raj: Back to results — last week's TTFT table you shared had 4 columns but some numbers looked like they were transcribed wrong, e.g., 1.4s vs 140ms. Can we get a clean table?
[04:24] Samantha: Sorry about that. I'll push a cleaned CSV with clarifying notes. The intended number was 140ms for streaming first token on small prompts.
[04:32] Jordan: Also, the model variant fallback — sometimes runtime swaps to a trimmed model when memory pressure rises. That can affect latency unpredictably. We recommend pinning a model variant for the pilot.
[04:44] Maya: How likely is the fallback in our expected load? Our p95 concurrency is about 60 concurrent sessions.
[04:50] Samantha: For 60 concurrent sessions with average seq length ~600, we might see memory pressure on a single GPU pod depending on model size. Options: increase node size, shard across pods, or use model quantization to reduce footprint.
[05:03] Raj: Can you summarize tradeoffs between quantization and TTFT?
[05:07] Samantha: Sure — INT8 reduces compute per token but adds dequant/decode overhead at token 1 which can slightly increase TTFT. But overall for sustained throughput it usually lowers p95 since kernels are faster. FP16 has lower first-token overhead but bigger kernel times for long sequences.
[05:22] Olivia: Any chance of mis-typing here — is INT8 always better for p95?
[05:26] Samantha: Not always. It depends on your prompt shapes. We'll validate with your traces.
[05:31] Jordan: We should also run kernel-level profiling with Nvidia Nsight or similar next week so infra can see where time is spent in matmuls vs attention.
[05:40] Samantha: Agreed. I propose: run microbenchmarks this week (Samantha), share cleaned CSVs (Samantha), Jordan to send security/pricing, Raj to share traces. Then kernel deep-dive with infra and NVIDIA on 2026-09-29.
[05:55] Raj: Sounds good. One more question — fallback to a smaller model variant, does Redwood do automated A/B rollback if quality drops?
[06:02] Jordan: Yes, we have rollouts with canary and auto-fallback if latency or quality thresholds are breached. We can enable canary for a small percentage of traffic.
[06:12] Maya: For the streaming chunk size, any recommended starting point?
[06:16] Samantha: Start with 32 tokens for chat, measure latency and tokens/sec. If first token is still high, try 16. There's a balance: smaller chunks reduce TTFT but increase overhead per chunk.
[06:28] Olivia: Okay, that's actionable. Anything else?
[06:31] Jordan: Quick recap — Samantha runs microbenchmarks + kernel selection logs; Jordan shares pricing and security; Raj uploads traces; schedule 9/29 profiling. We'll aim to meet AcmeFinance p95 target next week.
[06:44] Samantha: I'll also attach the runbook for kernel pinning and a short note on how to enable prefix caching safely.
[06:50] Olivia: Thanks, everyone. Appreciate the clarity.
[06:53] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up in Slack and with the deliverables.
[06:58] [meeting end]
